t: Largest 1-Bordered Square — Prefix Sums vs. Consecutive-Ones DP
o: We need the largest square subgrid whose *border* cells are all 1s; interior cells may be anything. The answer is the area (side squared) of that square, or 0 if no square of side ≥ 1 exists — note a single cell of value 1 already qualifies as a 1x1 bordered square, so Example 2 returns 1. In Example 1 the whole 3x3 grid has all-border 1s, so the answer is 9. With grids at most 100x100, even checking every candidate square naively is feasible if border checks are fast: there are O(n^3) candidate squares (top-left corner plus size), and we just need each border check to be O(1). Constraints also mean an O(n^3) solution is comfortably within limits.
k: A square is valid iff its four sides are all-1 runs; precompute run lengths so any side check is O(1).
For a fixed bottom-right cell, only squares whose side length is at most min(left-run, up-run) ending there can possibly be valid.
Answer is never 0 unless the grid contains no 1s at all, since every 1 is a valid 1x1 square.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with 2D Prefix Sums
a.i: Enumerate every top-left corner and every possible side length. A square of side s starting at (r,c) is valid iff its top row, bottom row, left column, and right column each contain s ones. Using a 2D prefix-sum array, the number of 1s in any segment of a row or column is computed in O(1), so each candidate is checked in O(1) after O(n^2) preprocessing.
s: Build prefix sums P where P[i][j] = sum of grid[0..i-1][0..j-1].
Define seg(r1,c1,r2,c2) to return the count of 1s in that inclusive rectangle in O(1).
For each top-left (r,c), iterate side s from min(m-r, n-c) down to 1 (largest first for early exit).
Check top row, bottom row, left column, right column sums equal s; if all pass, return s*s.
a.t: O(m*n*min(m,n)) — O(m^2) candidate corners, each trying up to min(m,n) sizes with O(1) checks via prefix sums.

a.i: For each cell compute left[i][j] = length of the run of 1s ending at (i,j) going left, and up[i][j] = run going up. Any valid square with bottom-right corner (i,j) and side s needs s <= left[i][j] and s <= up[i][j], but that's not sufficient — the far sides must also have long enough runs. So for each candidate s from min(left,up) downward, check whether left[i-s+1][j] >= s and up[i][j-s+1] >= s. This prunes heavily and avoids enumerating all sizes blindly.
s: Compute left[i][j]: 0 if grid is 0, else left[i][j-1] + 1.
Compute up[i][j]: 0 if grid is 0, else up[i-1][j] + 1.
For each cell (i,j), set limit = min(left[i][j], up[i][j]).
For s from limit down to current best+1, check left[i-s+1][j] >= s and up[i][j-s+1] >= s; if true, update best = s and stop.
a.t: O(m*n*min(m,n)) worst case, but typically much faster due to pruning by run lengths; preprocessing is O(m*n).
a.sp: O(m*n) for the two run-length tables.

w: In an interview, start with the brute-force idea, then immediately introduce prefix sums to make border checks O(1); mention the run-length DP as the polished optimal solution since it uses less memory per check and prunes aggressively. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a lone 1 counts as a valid answer (return s*s, not s); checking only left/up runs at the bottom-right corner without verifying the opposite sides; off-by-one errors when indexing the cell s steps away (use i-s+1, j-s+1). Edge cases: all zeros (answer 0), single cell, single row/column. Follow-ups might ask for the largest rectangle with 1-borders (harder, usually histogram-based) or handling very large grids where you'd want the same O(1)-check ideas with streaming computation.
